reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / GOLD & ATS guidelines
clinicalPearls: A group of parenchymal lung diseases caused by chronic inhalation of inorganic mineral dusts, most often occupational (coal, silica, asbestos, beryllium)
A detailed occupational and exposure history, including duration and intensity of dust contact and latency, is essential to diagnosis
Many patients are asymptomatic early, with disease detected on surveillance chest imaging before dyspnoea and cough develop
Chest radiography and CT typically show small rounded or irregular opacities, with characteristic patterns and distributions depending on the causative dust
Coal workers' pneumoconiosis ranges from simple disease with small nodules to progressive massive fibrosis with large conglomerate masses
There is no specific treatment to reverse the fibrosis; management centres on removal from exposure, supportive care, and prevention of complications
Asbestos exposure additionally raises the risk of pleural plaques, mesothelioma, and bronchogenic carcinoma, warranting long-term vigilance
Prevention through dust control, respiratory protection, and workplace exposure limits is the most effective strategy
reference.pathophysiology: Inhaled mineral dust particles that reach the distal airways and alveoli are engulfed by alveolar macrophages. Depending on particle size, surface reactivity, and burden, the macrophages are activated or killed, releasing inflammatory mediators, cytokines, and reactive oxygen species. Sustained exposure drives chronic inflammation and fibroblast activation, leading to collagen deposition, nodule formation, and, in advanced disease, coalescence into large fibrotic masses that distort lung architecture and impair gas exchange. The specific pattern reflects the fibrogenic potential of the particular dust.
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and other interstitial lung diseases
Pulmonary tuberculosis (which may also complicate pneumoconiosis)
Metastatic or miliary pulmonary nodular disease
Pulmonary manifestations of connective tissue disease
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiography, ideally read against standardised classification of pneumoconiosis opacities
High-resolution CT to characterise nodularity, fibrosis, and pleural disease
Pulmonary function testing to quantify restrictive, obstructive, or mixed impairment and gas transfer
Detailed occupational and environmental exposure documentation
Screening for complicating tuberculosis or, with asbestos, for malignancy where clinically indicated
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging masses or new nodules suggesting progressive massive fibrosis or malignancy
Constitutional symptoms or haemoptysis raising concern for tuberculosis or cancer
Rapid decline in lung function or new hypoxaemia
Pleural effusion or thickening in an asbestos-exposed patient suggesting mesothelioma
reference.prognosis: Simple pneumoconiosis may remain stable and cause little functional impairment, whereas progressive massive fibrosis and asbestos-related disease can lead to progressive respiratory failure; asbestos exposure carries a long-term risk of mesothelioma and lung cancer, and outcomes improve when further exposure is halted early.
pitfalls: Failing to take an adequate occupational history and therefore missing the diagnosis
Attributing all radiographic change to dust without excluding superimposed tuberculosis or malignancy
Assuming a short exposure excludes disease, given the often long latency
Overlooking the need to remove the worker from ongoing exposure
management: Remove the patient from further dust exposure, the single most important intervention, with workplace dust control and respiratory protection
Smoking cessation support given the amplified risk of functional impairment and malignancy
Supportive care with bronchodilators for coexisting airflow obstruction, pulmonary rehabilitation and long-term oxygen for chronic respiratory failure
Influenza and pneumococcal vaccination and prompt treatment of respiratory infections
Surveillance for and treatment of complicating tuberculosis, and vigilance for mesothelioma and lung cancer in asbestos-exposed patients
Serial chest imaging and pulmonary function testing to monitor progression
Occupational health involvement with compensation advice, and consideration of lung transplantation in end-stage disease
